SOURCE: "Natural-Language Agent Harnesses", Linyue Pan, Lexiao Zou, Shuo Guo, Jingchen Ni, Hai-Tao Zheng (Tsinghua SIGS; HIT Shenzhen). arXiv:2603.25723v2 [cs.CL], 18 May 2026. Preprint. Code: github.com/curated-skills/LinguaClaw.

COVERAGE: All 22 pages, 77,168 of 77,168 chars, read through the end (main text, references skimmed for origins, appendices A-G). No extraction faults. Table 8 text was fine. Tables 3-5 came out with flattened columns; I checked them against the prose.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Definition of harness (cleanest citable definition for note 01).
 number: none; lists 11 aspects
 setup: Section 2 Preliminaries; Table 8 gives a design question for each aspect.
 quote: "A harness is the external execution system around a model in an agent. It turns a base model into an agent that can act over real tasks by deciding what the model sees, what tools it may call, where state is stored, how observations are returned, when validation runs, how failures are recovered, when execution may stop, and how one or more model or agent calls are organized."
 where: p3
 Aspects (Table 8 / Sec 2): agent loop, tool design and documentation, context engineering, filesystem and workspace, memory and state, validation and stopping, safety/permissions/sandboxing, runtime defaults, observability/replay, retry/recovery, budget control. Note: the text says "eleven" and the list has eleven.
2. Core thesis: policy can be separated from mechanism. Natural language carries policy, code carries exact mechanism.
 number: none
 quote: "natural language carries the harness policy, while code and the runtime carry exact mechanisms such as tool execution, parsing, sandboxing, and logging."
 where: p2 (intro). Appendix A restates it: "This framing is narrower and more defensible than saying that natural language should replace controller code."
3. Static harness policy is much shorter as an NLAH than as code.
 number: Live-SWE 60.1k to 2.9k tokens; MHTBA 10.5k to 0.8k; SeeAct 47.5k to 1.4k
 setup: Table 2 counts static files, not runtime prompts or logs. Files: Live-SWE 68 code vs 3 NLAH; MHTBA 3 vs 1; SeeAct 5 vs 1.
 quote: "For Live-SWE, the readable harness policy is reduced from 60.1k tokens of code materials to a 2.9k-token NLAH. For MHTBA, it is reduced from 10.5k to 0.8k tokens."
 where: p6-7
4. Task performance comparable across code, prompted and IHR-executed NLAH (RQ1, Table 1).
 number: SWE-bench Verified (Live-SWE-Agent) Code 67.0 / Prompt 77.0 / NLAH 73.0. Terminal-Bench 2.0 (MHTBA) 36.0 / 57.3 / 53.9. OSWorld (SeeAct-style) 47.1 / 47.9 / 46.3.
 setup: one instantiation for all runs: Codex CLI 0.123.0, gpt-5.4-mini, reasoning effort xhigh, Docker, Ubuntu 24.04. Single attempt (Appendix C). No variance or seeds reported.
 quote: "On Live-SWE, IHR-executed NLAH reaches 73.0, above the native code harness at 67.0 and close to the prompted NLAH at 77.0. On OSWorld, NLAH reaches 46.3, essentially matching the code harness at 47.1. On MHTBA, NLAH reaches 53.9, below the prompted version at 57.3 but far above the native code realization at 36.0."
 where: p6
 Note: plain prompting of the same NLAH text beat IHR on SWE and TB2, so the paper does not show the runtime adds task gain over prompting. It adds auditable mechanisms.
5. A code harness tuned for one model transfers badly to another (Appendix C). This is directly relevant to the "co-training" and "state the model" points in the note.
 number: the MHTBA code score of 36.0 on TB2 is 32/89. 66 of 89 runs ended in AgentTimeoutError. 21 of those already had verifier reward 1.0. 45 failed with a timeout (50.6%).
 setup: MHTBA is the Meta-Harness TB2 artifact, optimized for Claude Opus 4.6. Here it was run under gpt-5.4-mini xhigh, one attempt.
 quote: "a code harness discovered for one model can encode latent assumptions about that model's tool-calling and stopping behavior, and those assumptions may be more fragile than the natural-language harness policy it was meant to implement."
 where: Appendix C, p15-16. Mechanism: a two-call task_complete stopping protocol. GPT answered "DONE" with no tool call, the controller issued a no-tool warning, the model ran a no-op, and the loop repeated until the 3600 s timeout (example task tune-mjcf: 186 episodes, 5.4M input tokens).
6. Module ablations: the modules that help are the ones that tighten state and acceptance (RQ3, Table 5).
 number: SWE Basic 73.0, OSWorld Basic 44.4.
 File-backed state: 75.6 (+2.6) / 58.3 (+13.9).
 Evidence-backed answering: 75.8 (+2.8) / 47.2 (+2.8).
 Verifier: 73.2 (+0.2) / 52.8 (+8.4).
 Self-evolution: 78.8 (+5.8) / 52.8 (+8.4).
 Multi-candidate search: 71.4 (-1.6) / 47.2 (+2.8).
 Dynamic orchestration: 74.6 (+1.6) / 47.2 (+2.8).
 Context compression: 72.0 (-1.0) / 36.1 (-8.3).
 Markdown memory: 70.2 (-2.8) / 50.0 (+5.6).
 setup: each row adds one module to a Basic condition under IHR, with the same model as above. Compare within a benchmark column only.
 quote: "File-backed state improves both benchmarks, from 73.0 to 75.6 on SWE and from 44.4 to 58.3 on OSWorld. Self-evolution is even stronger on the solve loop itself, reaching 78.8 on SWE and 52.8 on OSWorld."
 where: p8-9, Table 5 on p8
 Also: "Explicit NLAH modules are useful when they shorten the path from intermediate work to auditable evidence and final benchmark acceptance. They are less useful when they mainly add local process layers, extra branching, or compressed summaries whose notion of success can drift away from the evaluator."
7. More search is not better: multi-candidate search raised cost and lowered the SWE score.
 number: agent calls 1.1 to 5.7 on SWE; 1.083 to 1.333 on OSWorld.
 quote: "Agent Calls jump from 1.1 to 5.7 on SWE and from 1.083 to 1.333 on OSWorld, but this extra branching yields only +2.8 on OSWorld and a drop from 73.0 to 71.4 on SWE."
 where: p9
8. Durable path-addressable state beats aggressive compression.
 number: compression 73.0 to 72.0 on SWE; 44.4 to 36.1 on OSWorld.
 quote: "path-addressable durable state is a stronger and more reliable carrier than either aggressive summarization or free-form memory notes"
 where: Appendix F.1, p21
9. The verifier helps only when close to the benchmark's acceptance criterion.
 number: +0.2 SWE, +8.4 OSWorld
 quote: "It shows that an explicit checking stage can help, but only when the verifier's local object of judgment remains close to the benchmark's own acceptance criterion."
 where: p21
10. Runtime mechanism audit (RQ2, Table 4).
 number: Live-SWE NLAH: artifact contract 1.00, tool-call success 0.93, failed-tool continuation 0.99. MHTBA NLAH: 0.96 / 0.93 / 1.00. Handoff is the weak point: information handoff recall is 0.32 (SWE) and 0.55 (MHTBA) under parent-child execution, against 1.00 for prompted. Orchestration reliability is 0.83 and 0.85 against 1.00 and 0.99 for prompted.
 quote: "Information Handoff Recall drops from the direct-context Prompt setting to 0.322 and 0.553 under parent-child execution."
 where: p8
 Table 3: Verification Signals count is 9.89 for NLAH, 6.51 for Prompt, 3.99 for Code on SWE; 22.82, 13.18 and 45.05 on TB2. The NLAH text elsewhere says it "raises" Verification Signals on SWE only.
11. Cost overhead of NLAH over code (Table 1).
 number: Live-SWE LLM calls 23.3 (code) vs 41.0 (NLAH); tool calls 17.7 vs 63.4; prompt tokens 283.6k vs 2.2M. On TB2 the code harness used more: prompt tokens 10.4M vs 4.2M for NLAH, and 223.2 LLM calls vs 56.4.
 quote: "NLAHs often use more model calls, tool calls, or tokens than code harnesses." Wall-clock on SWE: code 28.9 min, NLAH 6.1 min.
 where: p6
12. Writing rules for harness documents (Section 3.2). These could feed the note's AGENTS.md discussion.
 quote: "Phrases such as 'be careful,' 'think deeply,' or 'act like an expert' are weak harness policy because they do not define observable behavior. By contrast, clauses such as 'write a state file before delegating,' 'run the verifier only after producing a candidate patch,' or 'do not finalize without evidence from the target file' are easier for IHR to execute and easier for researchers to audit."
 where: p4-5
 The four principles: state the task contract first; separate stages from mechanisms; make state and evidence explicit; write module boundaries so they can be ablated.
13. IHR architecture.
 number: 4 layers
 quote: "An NLAH+IHR system has four layers." The layers are base agent (an LLM loop whose only tool is a terminal), runtime policy (fixed instruction), NLAH (replaceable policy document), and scripts/adapters (deterministic code). Even a single-agent harness runs as a parent orchestrator plus one executor child.
 where: p3-4
14. Natural-language/code boundary (Table 9, Appendix D.2).
 quote: "Production systems should therefore keep safety, permissions, evaluation, and key parsing logic in code." Stated weaknesses of NLAH: "interpretation uncertainty, model dependence, cost, and safety or permission risks."
 where: p18

LIMITS
- The authors concede: "The main limitation is natural-language imprecision" (semantic constraints may be under-specified, read differently across models, or weakened by paraphrase) (p22).
- Security: harness text can carry prompt injection, malicious tool grafting and supply-chain contamination (p22).
- The runtime is a prototype. The authors call the overhead "an engineering target" and name handoff loss, fixed context overhead and redundant orchestration calls as open problems.
- Not shown, from my reading:
  - One model only (gpt-5.4-mini, xhigh) and one Codex CLI substrate. No cross-model replication of NLAH results.
  - Single attempt per task. No confidence intervals, seeds or significance. Several ablation deltas are small (+0.2, -1.0, -1.6), so treat them as noise-level.
  - No mid-run numbers are reported for the benchmark sample sizes, other than 89 TB2 tasks in Appendix C.
  - NLAH did not beat plain prompting on SWE or TB2. The code baselines are third-party artifacts that were not re-tuned for this model (Appendix C shows the MHTBA one fails mostly for a stopping-protocol reason).
  - No headline claim that NLAH improves accuracy. The abstract says only "comparable task outcomes".
  - Figure 1 mentions "self-harnessing" as a possible future design. This is not tested.
- Dated: gpt-5.4-mini, Codex CLI 0.123.0 and Claude Opus 4.6 are specific snapshots.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Harness and scaffold work: Yao et al., 2023 (ReAct); Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024b; Fourney et al., 2024 (Magentic-One); Anthropic, 2024 (Building effective agents); Anthropic 2025a (Effective harnesses for long-running agents); Anthropic 2025b (multi-agent research system); LangChain 2026a and 2026b; Bui, 2026; OpenAI 2026b (Harness engineering: leveraging codex).
- Meta-Harness: Lee et al., 2026 (the source of the MHTBA artifact).
- Instruction-carrier files: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, SKILL.md, AgentSkills (2026).
- Prompt programming: LMQL (Beurer-Kellner et al., 2023), DSPy (Khattab et al., 2024), APPL (Dong et al., 2025), SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024b).
- Workflow compilation: AutoFlow (Li et al., 2024) and others.
- Benchmarks: SWE-bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024; Chowdhury et al., 2024), Terminal-Bench 2.0 (Merrill et al., 2026), OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024).
- Live-SWE-Agent: Xia et al., 2025. SeeAct: Zheng et al., 2024a.
- Context-failure work: Liu et al., 2024 (Lost in the middle); Chroma Research, 2025 (context rot).

CODE: No code listings. Appendix F gives verbatim-style module spec boxes. Worth keeping:
- file-backed state: "No prompt, role instruction, reply, or promoted artifact counts as transferred until it exists as TASK.md, NLAH.md, RESPONSE.md, or another named file under STATE_ROOT." (p20)
- self-evolution: "default cap of five attempts", and "report incomplete to avoid pretending the last attempt passed." (p20)
- context compression: "never drop acceptance criteria, error signatures, commands still needed for replay, or handoff state." (p21)
- verifier: "Return exactly one primary verdict label plus a report ... and does not repair the candidate on its behalf." (p20)
- Runtime layout: STATE_ROOT (default /sa-output/runtime) holds durable state; /sa-output/artifacts holds judgeable deliverables. fork_context=true means the child inherits context; false means a fresh context with a minimal task packet (p19).

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p2): "Three ways to control an agent run." Spectrum from code harness (hard control) to NLAH+IHR to self-harnessing (no external harness). It positions the paper against code harnesses at a glance.
- Fig 2 (p3): "NLAH+IHR framework." Splits a native code harness (policy and mechanism mixed in controller code) into NLAH (policy), IHR (shared execution semantics) and scripts/adapters (mechanism). This is the best single picture of the policy/mechanism split.
- Tables 1, 2, 5 carry the main numbers. They are text tables, not figures.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found in the PDF text.
- Relation to note 01: the paper agrees with the note's definition, and gives an 11-aspect list that is broader than the note's 4 parts and 5 functions (it includes observability, budget control, runtime defaults). It does not support the note's "four parts" or the Agent = Model + Harness equation by name, and it does not report the LangChain 52.8 to 66.5 or Agent S4 figures (it cites LangChain 2026a/b only generically). The note's 52.8 to 66.5 and Agent S4 numbers are not in this paper, so they must not be attributed to it.
- The "Pan 2026" key in the filename matches first-author Pan. Version read is v2 (18 May 2026).
- Table 7 column headers wrapped in extraction. Its values are as given in Appendix C only for the first four slices; I did not quote the last column.
- The paper uses "Agent Calls" and "Perf." with the same column labels in Table 5. Read per benchmark.
